title: South Africa | Bank Governance, Board Training, Health and Safety, Harassment Prevention
tagline: From the boardroom to the branch floor: PA governance rules for directors, fit and proper checks, OHS Act duties and harassment prevention.
sectors: South African banks and controlling companies
Boards, board committees and company secretariats
Facilities, health and safety and branch management
description:
This quest teaches the South African rules that shape how a bank is governed and how it protects its people. It covers the **Banks Act** governance duties as restated by the **Prudential Authority (PA)** (sections 60, 60B and 64 to 64C), **PA Directive 1 of 2026** on governance and tenure (25 February 2026), which requires a board-approved policy ensuring **appropriate and ongoing training for directors** and ongoing assessment of each board member, the **fit and proper** rules for directors and executive officers including form BA 020 and **Directive 7 of 2022** on criminal background checks, the employer duties in the **Occupational Health and Safety Act** (including the section 8(2)(e) duty to provide information, instructions, training and supervision), and the **2022 Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Harassment in the Workplace** under the Employment Equity Act.

It is for directors, company secretaries, executives, HR, facilities and branch managers of South African banks. Director training is an express role-based duty under the PA Directive; OHS training is an express employer duty; harassment training is a good-practice expectation of the Code.

You follow a fictional team at Sable Crest Bank and study real cases from SARB and government sources.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your compliance, legal or HR teams.
audience: Directors, board committee chairs and company secretaries of South African banks and controlling companies
Executive officers and nominations or directors' affairs committee support staff
Human resources, employee relations and grievance handlers
Facilities, health and safety managers, representatives and branch managers
Compliance and internal audit staff who review governance and workplace controls
outcomes: Explain the Banks Act duties of directors and executive officers and the rules on board committees
Apply PA Directive 1 of 2026 on independence, tenure, director training and assessment
Apply the fit and proper rules, the BA 020 timing and the criminal background check requirements
Apply the OHS Act duties of employers, CEOs, employees and health and safety representatives
Recognise harassment and sexual harassment and apply the 2022 Code's policy, procedure and training expectations
Prepare honest evidence for governance and workplace reviews

quest.name: The Boardroom and the Branch Floor
quest.premise: You have just joined the company secretariat of Sable Crest Bank Limited, a fictional South African bank with its head office in Menlyn, Pretoria, a regional office in Cape Town and branches from East London to Durban. The Prudential Authority will review the bank's new governance policy next quarter. With company secretary Busisiwe Zulu, independent chair Hendrik Steyn, HR head Refilwe Mahlangu, health and safety manager Yusuf Cassim and branch manager Thabo Nkuna, clear five stages and then face the final review.

sessions.title: The Banks Act governance frame: duties, board and committees
sessions.summary: Learn who supervises bank governance, the personal duties of directors and executive officers, the non-executive majority, the section 60B governance process and the four statutory committees, with the VBS Mutual Bank failure as a warning.
objectives: Explain the Prudential Authority's role and its power to issue directives under section 6(6) of the Banks Act
Describe the duties in section 60 and the 49% cap on employee directors
Explain what the section 60B governance process must achieve
Identify the membership rules of the four statutory board committees

cards.title: Stage one: the empty chair
cards.setting: Board room, Sable Crest Bank head office, Menlyn, Pretoria. 07:50, before a board meeting.

lines.text: Your first day in the company secretariat of Sable Crest Bank Limited, a fictional South African bank. Twelve chairs face a long table. One has a fresh name card.
Welcome! I'm Busisiwe Zulu, company secretary. That new card belongs to a director who joins us today. Your job this quarter is the board's governance file.
Hendrik Steyn, independent chair. The Prudential Authority reviews our governance policy next quarter, and it now asks how we train directors, not only who we appoint.
Refilwe Mahlangu, HR and employee relations. Governance isn't only the boardroom. The PA looks at the board; the Labour department looks at how we treat and protect staff.
Yusuf Cassim, facilities and health and safety, Cape Town. And my inspectors ask a simple question: did you inform, instruct, train and supervise your people?
Thabo Nkuna, branch manager in East London. Honestly, the branch floor feels a long way from this table.
It isn't. Five stages: the Banks Act, the new Directive on governance, fit and proper people, health and safety, and harassment. Stage one: what does the law expect a bank board to do?

cards.title: The Banks Act governance frame in five scenes

scenes.heading: The prudential supervisor
scenes.narration: The Prudential Authority, inside the South African Reserve Bank, supervises banks for safety and soundness. Under section 6(6) of the Banks Act it can issue directives that banks must follow.

scenes.heading: Personal duties
scenes.narration: Section 60 says each director, chief executive officer and executive officer owes the bank a fiduciary duty and a duty of care and skill. The duty is personal, not just collective.

scenes.heading: A mostly non-executive board
scenes.narration: The same section caps employees at 49 per cent of a bank's directors, rounded down. In practice, most directors must be non-executive.

scenes.heading: A real governance process
scenes.narration: Section 60B makes the board and executive officers responsible for an adequate and effective corporate governance process that fits the nature, complexity and risks of the bank's business.

scenes.heading: Committees with teeth
scenes.narration: Sections 64 to 64C require an audit committee, a risk and capital management committee, a directors' affairs committee and a remuneration committee, each with rules on who may sit on it.

cards.title: The four statutory board committees

items.label: Audit (s 64)
items.left: Members may not be employees of the bank or its group
items.right: The board chair may not be a member

items.label: Risk and capital (s 64A)
items.right: At least two must be non-executive

items.label: Directors' affairs (s 64B)
items.right: Reviews governance and board continuity and skills

items.label: Remuneration (s 64C)
items.right: Oversees how the bank pays its people

cards.caption: Summarised from Annexure A to PA Directive 1 of 2026, which restates these Banks Act sections for ease of reference.

cards.question: Sable Crest's board has 12 directors. Under section 60 of the Banks Act, what is the largest number who may be employees of the bank or its group?
cards.explanation: The cap is 49 per cent rounded down to the next whole number. 49 per cent of 12 is 5.88, which rounds down to 5. Six would already be half the board, which the rule is designed to prevent.

cards.title: Section 60B: what the governance process is for
Match the Banks Act section to its duty
cards.prompt: Link each section to what it requires.

pairs.right: Fiduciary duty and duty of care and skill; employees capped at 49% of directors
An adequate and effective governance process suited to the bank's risks
Audit committee of non-employees, without the board chair
Risk and capital management committee of at least three, two non-executive
Directors' affairs committee: governance review, continuity and skills mix

lines.text: Before you design anything, read this. It's the Reserve Bank's statement from March 2018 on VBS Mutual Bank.
The Governor said the bank's problems came from a failure of the board and executive management to manage rapid growth, funding and liquidity.
So it wasn't a market crash. It was the people at the table.
Exactly. Every rule you'll study this quest is somebody's lesson learned the hard way.

cards.title: Real case: VBS Mutual Bank, 2017-2018
cards.body:
**What happened (from SARB statements):**

- **August 2017:** the SARB imposed administrative sanctions on VBS for weaknesses in its FIC Act controls: a R2.5 million penalty (R2 million suspended on conditions) and a directive to fix customer identification and reporting processes.
- **11 March 2018:** the Minister of Finance placed VBS under curatorship. The Governor said its liquidity crisis came from the board's and management's failure to manage rapid growth and funding, including short-term municipal deposits lent out long-term. The board and management lost their powers to the curator.
- **April 2018:** the PA appointed Advocate Terry Motau SC to investigate under section 134 of the FSR Act.
- **July 2018:** government guaranteed retail deposits up to R100,000, paid through Nedbank; the SARB estimated about 97% of some 22,700 retail depositors would be repaid in full.
- **October 2018:** the investigator reported that almost R2 billion had been taken.

VBS was a mutual bank under its own Act, but the governance lesson applies to every bank.

cards.title: The growth slide
cards.situation: At a board meeting, the head of treasury presents a plan to grow deposits fast by taking large short-term deposits from a few public-sector clients and lending them out on long terms. Profits look excellent. Two non-executive directors look at their phones. The chair asks if there are questions. You are taking minutes.

choices.text: Prompt the chair, through the company secretary, to ask the risk and capital committee for a liquidity and concentration analysis before approval.
choices.outcome: Best. Section 60B expects decisions within acceptable risk limits, and the risk and capital committee exists for exactly this. The minutes will show the board challenged the plan. VBS showed where unchallenged concentrated funding can lead.

choices.text: Record that the board approved the plan, since nobody objected.
choices.outcome: Poor. Silence is not oversight. Directors owe a duty of care and skill; minutes showing no challenge to a risky plan are evidence against the board later.

choices.text: Email the non-executive directors after the meeting to suggest they read the plan more carefully.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Raising the concern helps, but the decision has already been taken. The time to test the risk was before approval, through the proper committee route.

cards.title: VBS Mutual Bank: from warning to failure

items.label: Penalty for weak controls
items.detail: SARB sanctions VBS over FIC Act control weaknesses: R2.5 million, R2 million suspended.

items.label: Curatorship
items.detail: Minister places VBS under curatorship; board and management relieved of their powers.

items.label: Forensic investigation
items.detail: PA appoints an investigator under section 134 of the FSR Act.

items.label: Depositors repaid
items.detail: Retail deposits up to R100,000 repaid through Nedbank under a government guarantee.

items.label: Investigator's report
items.detail: Report to the PA finds almost R2 billion was taken from the bank.

cards.caption: Dates and amounts from SARB media statements of 4 August 2017, 11 March, 13 April, 9 July and 10 October 2018.

cards.title: Governance words you'll hear all quest

cards.back: A duty to act in good faith in the bank's interests, not your own; directors and executive officers owe it personally.
A duty to bring proper attention, diligence and competence to the role, including understanding what you approve.
A senior manager defined in the Banks Act; the PA treats executive management and senior executive management the same way.
The holding company registered as controlling a bank; most governance rules apply to it as well as to the bank.
A binding instruction the PA issues to banks under the Banks Act, such as Directive 1 of 2026 on governance.
When a curator takes over management of a failing bank and the board's powers pass to the curator.

cards.question: Which statement about section 60B of the Banks Act is accurate?
options: Only the board chair is responsible for the governance process
The board and executive officers must keep an effective governance process that fits the bank's risks
It applies only to banks listed on the stock exchange
It lists the exact number of board meetings a year
cards.explanation: Section 60B puts the duty on the board and the executive officers together, and ties the process to the nature, complexity and risks of the bank's business. It does not single out the chair or depend on a listing.

cards.title: Minutes are your evidence
cards.body: Supervisors judge governance by what the record shows. Good minutes capture the **questions** directors asked, the **information** they relied on, any **conflicts declared** and **who abstained**. A one-line "approved" tells a reviewer nothing about care and skill.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The PA supervises banks and issues binding directives under section 6(6) of the Banks Act.
Directors, the CEO and executive officers each owe the bank a fiduciary duty and a duty of care and skill (s 60).
Employees may make up at most 49% of a bank's board, rounded down, so most directors are non-executive.
Section 60B requires an effective governance process that includes ethics, conflict management and compliance with all laws.
VBS Mutual Bank (2018) shows how board failure to manage growth and funding can end in curatorship.

cards.prompt: Think about a decision your own board or senior team approved recently. If a supervisor read the minutes, could they see the questions asked and the risks weighed?

quiz.question: Which body supervises South African banks for safety and soundness and issues directives under the Banks Act?
options: The Financial Sector Conduct Authority
The Prudential Authority in the South African Reserve Bank
The Financial Sector Conduct Authority, as twin-peaks lead regulator
The Commission for Employment Equity
quiz.explanation: The Prudential Authority sits in the SARB and is the prudential regulator of banks; Directive 1 of 2026 was issued under section 6(6) of the Banks Act. The FSCA regulates conduct, and the Labour department administers workplace laws.

quiz.question: Under section 60 of the Banks Act, who owes a bank a fiduciary duty and a duty of care and skill?
options: Only the non-executive directors who sit on statutory board committees
Only the chair of the board and the company secretary
The controlling company's shareholders, as owners
Each director, the chief executive officer and each executive officer
quiz.explanation: Section 60, as restated in Annexure A to Directive 1 of 2026, names each director, the CEO and each executive officer. The duty is personal and is not limited to committee members or the chair.

quiz.question: A bank has a board of 15 directors. Applying the section 60 cap, how many of them may at most be employees of the bank or its group?
quiz.explanation: 49% of 15 is 7.35, rounded down to 7. Eight would be more than half of the board; the rule's purpose is a non-executive majority.

quiz.question: The board of Sable Crest Bank wants to appoint its chair to the audit committee because she is a chartered accountant. What does the Banks Act, as summarised in Annexure A, say?
options: The chair may join if the PA approves her qualifications in writing first
The chair may join but may not chair the committee
The board chair may not be a member of the audit committee
The chair may join if most members are non-executive
quiz.explanation: Section 64 bars the chair of the board (of the bank or its controlling company) from audit committee membership, regardless of qualifications. The other options describe conditions the Act does not offer.

quiz.question: What is the minimum make-up of a bank's risk and capital management committee under section 64A?
options: At least five members, all of them independent
At least two members, one of them the chief risk officer
At least three board members, at least two of them non-executive
Any number, provided the chair is non-executive
quiz.explanation: Section 64A requires at least three board members, of whom at least two are non-executive directors. The other options invent numbers or roles.

quiz.question: Which committee must help the board run a directorship continuity programme that includes regularly reviewing the board's mix of skills and experience?
options: The directors' affairs committee
The audit committee
The remuneration committee
The risk and capital management committee
quiz.explanation: Section 64B gives the directors' affairs committee, made up only of non-executive directors, the role of assessing governance and supporting continuity and a regular skills review.

quiz.question: A director says: 'Section 60B is about strategy and profit; labour and safety law is HR's problem.' Why is that wrong?
options: Section 60B makes HR directors personally liable for all labour law
Section 60B transfers responsibility for labour inspections to the Prudential Authority
Section 60B requires every director to qualify in labour law
One aim of the s 60B process is compliance with all applicable laws
quiz.explanation: One of the stated aims of the section 60B process is compliance with all applicable laws, which includes employment and safety law. It does not move inspections to the PA or create an HR-only liability.

quiz.question: According to the SARB Governor's statement of 11 March 2018, what caused VBS Mutual Bank's liquidity crisis?
options: A sudden national banking crisis that hit every mutual bank in the country at once
Board and management failure to manage growth, funding and liquidity
A cyber attack that froze the bank's payment systems
A court order freezing municipal accounts
quiz.explanation: The Governor tied the crisis to the board and executive management failing to manage growth, funding and liquidity, including short-term municipal deposits lent long-term. The SARB stressed the wider banking system was sound.

quiz.question: In August 2017, months before VBS was placed under curatorship, the SARB imposed sanctions on it. What was the reason given?
options: Weaknesses in its FIC Act anti-money laundering controls
Failing to hold board meetings for a year
Paying directors more than the legal maximum
Breaching the 49% cap on executive directors
quiz.explanation: The 4 August 2017 statement says the sanctions (R2.5 million, R2 million suspended, plus remedial directives) were for weak FIC Act control measures. It was an early warning sign of weak oversight.

quiz.question: Minutes of a Sable Crest board meeting say only: 'Expansion plan approved.' Why would a supervisor see this as a weakness?
options: Minutes must be signed by every director to be valid
The PA requires minutes to be published on the bank's website
It shows no evidence that directors used care and skill or challenged risk
Board decisions are invalid unless a PA official attended and signed the minutes too
quiz.explanation: Directors owe a duty of care and skill and must keep an effective governance process. Minutes are the record of how they exercised it; a bare approval shows no questioning. The other statements are not Banks Act rules.

sessions.title: PA Directive 1 of 2026: independence, tenure, training and assessment
sessions.summary: Unpack the PA's 2026 governance Directive: what the board-approved policy must contain, the tests that deem a director not independent, the nine-year tenure rule and its exceptions, ongoing director training and assessment, and how the PA supervises it.
objectives: Explain the status, scope and date of PA Directive 1 of 2026
Apply the minimum tests that deem a director not independent
Work through the nine-year tenure, extension, cooling-off and reappointment rules
Design board training and assessment that meet paragraphs 7.1.3.6 and 7.1.3.7

lines.text: Our longest-serving independent director, Mrs Govender, reaches nine years on the board in March. She's our best credit mind.
Then Directive 1 of 2026 matters. The PA issued it on 25 February 2026 and it replaces Directive 4 of 2018.
Does she have to leave the board?
Not necessarily. But the Directive changes what we may call her, and what our board policy must say about tenure, independence and training.
Training? Directors get training too?
They must. The policy has to ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors. That's our second stage: build a policy the PA will accept.

scenes.heading: What it is
scenes.narration: Directive 1 of 2026 was issued by the Prudential Authority under section 6(6) of the Banks Act on 25 February 2026. It replaces Directive 4 of 2018 and focuses on governance and the tenure of independent directors.

scenes.heading: Who it binds
scenes.narration: It is addressed to banks and controlling companies. They must have, and actually implement, a sufficiently robust board-approved policy. It does not apply to the board of a foreign bank operating a branch in South Africa.

scenes.heading: Independence
scenes.narration: The policy must protect board independence: an independent non-executive chair, independent chairs of the required board sub-committees, and cooling-off periods before former insiders can become non-executive directors.

scenes.heading: Tests for independence
scenes.narration: It must contain objective tests that deem a director not independent, for example a substantial shareholding, performance-linked pay, recent executive roles or nine years as an independent director.

scenes.heading: Training and assessment
scenes.narration: The policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors and ongoing assessment of how effective each board member is. This is the express training duty of the Directive.

scenes.heading: Supervision
scenes.narration: The PA assesses the policy and how it works in practice during its supervisory review, and can require the bank to fix deficiencies within a period it sets in writing.

cards.title: What the board-approved policy must cover

items.label: Protect independence
items.detail: Independent chair and sub-committee chairs; cooling-off for former insiders.

items.label: Test independence
items.detail: Objective tests that deem a director not independent.

items.label: Select and compose
items.detail: Rigorous selection, continuity, enough independent directors, effective oversight.

items.label: Train and assess
items.detail: Appropriate and ongoing director training; ongoing assessment of each member.

items.label: Specify limits
items.detail: Maximum boards per non-executive, annual independence declarations, fit and proper criteria.

items.label: Prevent conflicts
items.detail: Stop clashes between the bank's interests and directors' personal interests.

cards.caption: A summary of paragraph 7.1 of Directive 1 of 2026, in our own words.

cards.question: Which paragraph of Directive 1 of 2026 carries the express duty about directors' training?
options: Paragraph 7.1.3.6: the policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors
Paragraph 7.4: training is optional for foreign branches
Paragraph 2.1: the PA trains every new director itself
Paragraph 8.1: auditors must train the board each year
cards.explanation: Paragraph 7.1.3.6 requires the board-approved policy to ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors; 7.1.3.7 adds ongoing assessment of individual effectiveness. The PA does not run the training itself.

cards.title: Deemed not independent: the main tests
Independent or deemed not independent?
cards.prompt: Sort each director using the Directive's minimum tests.

items.text: Receives only directors' fees and served four years
Holds 7% of the voting rights with her associates
Was the bank's chief financial officer two years ago
Was the CFO of a different, unrelated company until last year
Receives share options that vest on the bank's profit targets
Her brother is the bank's chief executive
Was a partner at the bank's statutory auditor five years ago
Has completed nine years as an independent director

lines.text: Mrs Govender reaches nine years in March. From then, if we keep her, she counts as a non-executive director but not an independent one.
That leaves our credit committee one independent member short.
There is one exception. In exceptional cases the PA may approve, in writing, an extension of the nine years, for up to 24 months, with conditions.
So we either plan her successor, or we make a real case to the PA. We can't just assume.

cards.title: Keeping Mrs Govender
cards.situation: Mrs Govender will complete nine years as an independent non-executive director in March. The board wants her expertise. The credit committee needs an independent chair. It is now November.

choices.text: Start succession for the committee chair now, and decide whether there is an exceptional case to ask the PA in writing for an extension of up to 24 months.
choices.outcome: Best. The Directive lets the PA approve an extension of up to 24 months only in exceptional cases and in writing. Planning a successor in parallel protects the committee either way.

choices.text: Keep her as independent chair of the committee; nine years is only a guideline.
choices.outcome: Poor. After nine years she is deemed not independent unless the PA has approved an extension. Chairing a required sub-committee as an 'independent' would breach the board's own policy and the Directive.

choices.text: Ask her to resign in February and reappoint her in June so the nine-year clock restarts.
choices.outcome: Poor. The Directive closes this gap: a director who resigns before completing the tenure and returns within three years only gets the remaining years of her original nine, so the clock does not restart.

choices.text: Keep her on the board as a non-executive director but move the committee chair to another independent director.
choices.outcome: Partly right. This works from March without PA approval. But it should be planned now with the directors' affairs committee, and the board must check it still has enough independent directors.

cards.title: Numbers in Directive 1 of 2026

items.label: Independent tenure
items.detail: After nine years an independent director is treated as non-independent unless the PA approves an extension.

items.label: Maximum PA extension
items.detail: Exceptional cases only, approved in writing, with conditions.

items.label: Cooling-off to join as NED
items.detail: Former executive, CEO, executive officer, statutory auditor or curator, unless the PA allows less.

items.label: Recent insider test
items.detail: Executive roles, curator, or material adviser in this period mean not independent.

items.label: Substantial shareholder
items.detail: Holding with associates above this share of nominal value or voting rights.

cards.caption: All figures from paragraph 7.1 of Directive 1 of 2026 (25 February 2026).

cards.title: Match the policy element to its purpose
cards.prompt: Each item comes from paragraph 7.1 of the Directive.

pairs.right: Keeps leadership of the board separate from management and major interests
A fallback channel when the chair is conflicted or temporarily not independent
Made at the first board meeting each financial year and whenever circumstances change
Makes sure each non-executive has enough time for the bank
Keeps directors' knowledge current for the bank's business and risks

cards.question: An independent director's circumstances change mid-year: her husband joins the bank's main external consultancy as a partner. What does the Directive expect?
options: Nothing until the next annual review
A fresh independence declaration, which the bank must assess and verify
Automatic removal from the board by the PA
A new form BA 020 within 30 days
cards.explanation: The declaration is due at the first meeting each financial year and whenever circumstances change that may affect independence, and the bank must assess and verify it. The PA does not remove directors automatically.

cards.title: Make training evidence-ready
cards.body: Keep a **training log per director**: induction topics, ongoing sessions (for example new directives, cyber, conduct, labour and safety risks), dates and attendance. Link it to the **annual board effectiveness review** so gaps found in assessment become next year's training. That is how you show the policy is implemented, not just approved.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Directive 1 of 2026 (25 February 2026) replaces Directive 4 of 2018 and requires a robust, implemented board-approved governance policy.
The chair and the chairs of required sub-committees must be independent non-executive directors, with narrow PA exceptions.
After nine years an independent director counts as non-independent; the PA may extend by up to 24 months in exceptional cases, in writing.
The policy must ensure appropriate and ongoing director training and ongoing assessment of each board member.
The PA assesses policy and practice in its supervisory review and can order deficiencies fixed.

cards.prompt: If you sat on a board, which topics would you need training on in the next 12 months to challenge management with confidence?

quiz.question: Which earlier directive does PA Directive 1 of 2026 replace?
options: Directive 7 of 2022
Directive 4 of 2023
Directive 14 of 2025
Directive 4 of 2018
quiz.explanation: The Directive states that it replaces Directive 4 of 2018 on governance. Directive 7 of 2022 deals with criminal background checks and remains separate.

quiz.question: To which of these does Directive 1 of 2026 NOT apply?
options: The board of a foreign institution running a bank branch in South Africa
A South African bank's board
A controlling company's board
A bank whose chair is temporarily conflicted
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.4 excludes the board of a foreign institution conducting banking business in South Africa through an authorised branch. Banks and controlling companies are covered.

quiz.question: Which pair of requirements in the Directive deals directly with directors' development and performance?
options: An annual exam set by the PA, and a pass mark for each director
Training only at induction, and a peer review every five years
Ongoing training for directors and ongoing assessment of each board member
Training for executive directors only, plus an assessment of the board by the external auditors
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 7.1.3.6 and 7.1.3.7 require the policy to ensure appropriate and ongoing training for directors and ongoing assessment of individual board members. The Directive sets no PA exam.

quiz.question: Mr Dlamini owns 4% of Sable Crest's shares and his company owns another 2%. Is he deemed not independent under the substantial shareholder test?
options: No, because only his personal 4% counts
Yes, because holdings with associates are added and together exceed 5%
No, because the test only applies above 10%
Yes, because any shareholder is deemed not independent
quiz.explanation: The substantial shareholder test counts the person's shares together with those of associates; 6% is more than 5%. Holding shares alone below the threshold would not breach this test.

quiz.question: A non-executive director is paid fees plus share options that vest when the bank hits profit targets. What is the effect under the Directive?
options: She stays independent because share options are a normal part of directors' pay packages
She stays independent if the remuneration committee approves the options
She is independent until the options actually vest
She is not independent because her pay is linked to the bank's performance
quiz.explanation: Pay other than directors' fees or directors' remuneration that is contingent on the bank's performance, such as a share incentive, makes a director not independent. Approval or timing does not change that.

quiz.question: Sable Crest's former chief financial officer, an executive officer as defined in the Banks Act, retired eight months ago. The board wants him as a non-executive director now. What does the Directive say?
options: He can be appointed at once as an independent director
Not within 12 months, unless the PA allows a shorter period in an exceptional case
He can never again be appointed to the board of the bank where he was an executive officer
He can be appointed only after nine years
quiz.explanation: A former executive officer faces a 12-month cooling-off before appointment as a non-executive director, with a PA discretion to shorten it in exceptional cases. Even after that, the three-year test means he would not count as independent yet.

quiz.question: An independent director resigned after six years and is reappointed two years later. How is her independent tenure counted?
options: Her remaining three years of the nine apply from reappointment
The nine-year clock restarts from zero
She can no longer be treated as independent at all, because she broke her term
The two years away are added to her tenure
quiz.explanation: If an independent director resigns before completing the tenure and returns within three years, only the remaining years of the original nine apply from reappointment. This stops the clock being reset by short breaks.

quiz.question: When must an independent director give a declaration that she meets the board's independence criteria?
options: Only once, on appointment
Every quarter, in a signed declaration sent to the Prudential Authority directly
At her first meeting, at the first meeting each financial year and on any change
Only when the PA requests it in writing
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.1.4.2 sets these three trigger points, and the bank must assess and verify the content of the declaration as part of its own governance process.

quiz.question: During its supervisory review, the PA finds that Sable Crest's governance policy does not cover director training. What may the PA do under the Directive?
options: Nothing, because director training is a voluntary matter for King Code guidance only
Fine each director a fixed amount set in the Directive
Automatically suspend the bank's licence
Require the bank to fix it within a period the PA directs in writing
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.3 lets the PA require deficiencies to be corrected within the period it directs in writing. The Directive does not set fixed fines or automatic suspension.

quiz.question: Why must the policy limit the number and type of other boards a non-executive director may sit on?
options: So that directors' fees stay below a national cap
So each director can give enough time to properly discharge duties at the bank
Because the Companies Act bans multiple directorships for anyone who chairs a committee
So the PA can keep its register of directors short
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.1.4.1 links the limit to each director's circumstances and the nature, scale and complexity of their directorships, so they can devote enough time to the bank.

sessions.title: Fit and proper directors and executive officers
sessions.summary: Follow a new director from nomination to induction: the Banks Act fit and proper qualities, form BA 020 and its 30-day rule, criminal background checks under Directive 7 of 2022, the VBS lesson on integrity, and a training and assessment cycle for the board.
objectives: Explain the fit and proper qualities in section 1(1A) of the Banks Act and the bank's own responsibility
Apply the BA 020 timing rules for first appointments and reappointments
Apply the criminal background check rules in Directive 7 of 2022
Build a director development cycle linking skills reviews, training, assessment and re-screening

cards.title: Stage three: the new director's file

lines.text: The nominations work starts today. Dr Sizwe Mabuza is the board's choice for a new non-executive seat. He has never been a bank director.
Strong CV. Former deputy vice-chancellor, sat on two audit committees.
A CV isn't a fit and proper assessment. We assess before appointment, and the PA must get his BA 020 with a criminal background check report well before he takes the seat.
And once he's in, our new governance policy says he gets an induction and ongoing training. So who designs that?
We do. Stage three: fit and proper people, from nomination to their training plan.

cards.title: Fit and proper in five scenes

scenes.heading: The three qualities
scenes.narration: Section 1(1A) of the Banks Act tells the PA to consider three qualities, as far as it can reasonably determine them: the person's general probity, their competence and soundness of judgement for the office, and the diligence they are likely to bring.

scenes.heading: The bank's own responsibility
scenes.narration: Directive 7 of 2022 is clear: banks are ultimately responsible for choosing fit and proper directors and senior managers, and must assess them before appointment and regularly afterwards.

scenes.heading: Form BA 020
scenes.narration: Regulation 42 requires a completed form BA 020, a statement of the person's attributes, with a CV. The chair or the chair's representative submits it, or the auditor for a new bank.

scenes.heading: Thirty days ahead
scenes.narration: For a first appointment as director or executive officer, the form goes to the PA at least 30 days before the appointment takes effect. The same applies when someone returns more than 12 months after resigning.

scenes.heading: Background checks
scenes.narration: Since 1 September 2022 every BA 020 for a prospective or interim person must come with a criminal background check report. A person who will not or cannot be checked is disqualified.

cards.title: What fit and proper means at a bank

items.label: Probity
items.detail: Honesty, integrity and a clean record: no criminal or regulatory history that makes the person unfit.

items.label: Competence and judgement
items.detail: Knowledge, proportionate skills and experience for the role and the bank's risks.

items.label: Diligence
items.detail: Time, attention and commitment to actually do the job.

items.label: Independence of mind
items.detail: Especially for non-executive directors: willing to challenge management.

cards.caption: The first three are the Banks Act section 1(1A) qualities; independence of mind is part of selection under Directive 1 of 2026.

cards.question: Which statement best reflects Directive 7 of 2022 on who is responsible for appointing fit and proper directors?
options: The PA chooses directors and the bank confirms them
The bank is ultimately responsible and must assess before and regularly after appointment
Shareholders alone are responsible at the annual general meeting
The external auditor certifies each director as fit and proper
cards.explanation: Paragraph 1.1 of Directive 7 of 2022 puts ultimate responsibility on the bank, with due diligence before appointment and on a regular basis afterwards. The PA reviews the information; it does not choose directors.

cards.title: Criminal background checks: the Directive 7 of 2022 rules
cards.body:
Directive 7 of 2022 (12 August 2022) adds a **criminal background check report (CBCR)** to the fit and proper process. In summary:

- From **1 September 2022**, every BA 020 for a prospective or interim director or executive officer must include a CBCR.
- A CBCR for a **South African national** may be no older than **30 calendar days** when the BA 020 is submitted; for a **foreign national**, no older than **60 calendar days**.
- Anyone **unable or unwilling** to undergo a check is **disqualified** from appointment.
- Banks must **re-screen** serving directors, executive officers and key persons periodically and send the reports to the PA within **30 calendar days** of completing the screening; the PA may also ask at any time.
- The rule also covers appointments in the group's cross-border banking operations and applications to establish a new bank.

A police clearance certificate, or a report from a provider with an arrangement with the police, is acceptable.

cards.title: Appointing a new non-executive director
cards.prompt: Put the steps in a sensible order for Dr Mabuza's appointment.
steps: Directors' affairs committee reviews the board's skills gaps and agrees the profile needed
Nominee is assessed against the policy's fit and proper and independence criteria
Criminal background check report is obtained (not older than 30 days for a South African)
Chair submits form BA 020 with CV and report to the PA at least 30 days before appointment
Appointment takes effect and the director gives an independence declaration at the first meeting
Induction programme starts and the director's training log is opened

lines.text: Dr Mabuza's BA 020 draft says 'no' to every question. But his background check shows a 2009 conviction for drunk driving.
He says he forgot about it. It was a long time ago.
The conviction may not disqualify him on its own. The failure to disclose is a probity question in itself.
We don't decide this by guessing. We correct the form, assess it honestly and let the PA see the full picture.

cards.title: The undisclosed conviction
cards.situation: Dr Mabuza's criminal background check shows an old conviction he did not disclose on the draft BA 020. The board is keen to appoint him next month. You are preparing the submission to the PA.

choices.text: Ask Dr Mabuza to correct the BA 020, record the board's assessment of both the conviction and the non-disclosure, and submit the full file to the PA.
choices.outcome: Best. The bank is responsible for honest assessment, and the PA considers probity. A complete, corrected file lets everyone judge the facts. Hiding it would itself be a governance failure.

choices.text: Submit the draft as it is, with the check report attached; the PA can spot it.
choices.outcome: Poor. The chair signs the submission. Sending a form the bank knows is inaccurate undermines the bank's own fit and proper responsibility and the chair's credibility.

choices.text: Withdraw the nomination immediately without discussing it with him.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Caution is understandable, but a single old conviction is not an automatic bar. The board should assess it fairly, including the non-disclosure, and decide on facts.

cards.title: Real case: the VBS investigator on board integrity

cards.back: The prescribed statement of a serving or prospective director's or executive officer's attributes, sent to the PA with a CV.
Criminal background check report: a police clearance or approved provider report on a person's criminal status.
The Banks Act provision listing probity, competence and judgement, and diligence as the qualities the PA considers.
Periodic fresh checks on serving directors and executives; reports go to the PA within 30 calendar days.
The PA may require a BA 020 for a director already in office.

cards.title: The director development cycle

items.label: Skills review
items.detail: Directors' affairs committee maps skills against strategy and risks.

items.label: Induction
items.detail: Banking law, the bank's business model, risk appetite and key policies.

items.label: Ongoing training
items.detail: Planned sessions on new rules and emerging risks, logged per director.

items.label: Individual assessment
items.detail: Ongoing review of each member's effectiveness.

items.label: Re-screening
items.detail: Periodic background checks and independence declarations.

cards.caption: Combines Banks Act s 64B, Directive 1 of 2026 (7.1.3.6-7.1.3.7, 7.1.4.2) and Directive 7 of 2022 (2.1.13).

cards.question: Sable Crest wants to reappoint a former director who resigned 14 months ago. What does regulation 42, as described in Directive 1 of 2026, require?
options: No new form, because he has served before
A BA 020 at least 30 days before the reappointment takes effect
A BA 020 within 30 days after he takes his seat
Only a fresh independence declaration
cards.explanation: A person reappointed more than 12 months after resigning is treated like a first-time appointee: the BA 020 must reach the PA at least 30 days before the appointment takes effect.

cards.title: Training plans that pass review
cards.body: Tie each director's plan to **three inputs**: the skills matrix, the individual effectiveness assessment and the bank's **regulatory calendar** (new directives, joint standards, labour and safety law). Include topics the whole board needs, such as the duties in this quest. Record attendance, and follow up on missed sessions.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: The PA considers probity, competence and soundness of judgement, and diligence (Banks Act s 1(1A)).
Banks are ultimately responsible for assessing directors and executives before appointment and regularly afterwards.
Form BA 020 goes to the PA at least 30 days before a first appointment, with a criminal background check report.
Background check reports may be at most 30 days old for South Africans and 60 days for foreign nationals.
Ongoing training, assessment and re-screening turn fit and proper from a gate into a cycle.

cards.prompt: What would you want to know about a new colleague in a position of trust before they start, and what should be checked again after a few years?

quiz.question: Which three qualities does section 1(1A) of the Banks Act tell the PA to consider when deciding if a director is fit and proper?
options: Age, nationality and years of banking experience
Shareholding, independence and remuneration
General probity, competence and soundness of judgement, and diligence
Formal qualifications, official language skills and past board attendance records
quiz.explanation: Directive 1 of 2026 restates section 1(1A): probity, competence and soundness of judgement for the role, and the diligence the person is likely to show. The other lists are not the statutory qualities.

quiz.question: Who normally submits form BA 020 to the PA for a proposed director of an existing bank?
options: The chair of the board or the chair's duly appointed representative
The proposed director personally
The bank's external auditor
The head of human resources
quiz.explanation: Regulation 42 requires the chair or the chair's representative to submit the form; the auditor does so only for a new bank.

quiz.question: Sable Crest plans to appoint a first-time executive officer on 1 June. What is the latest date the BA 020 can reach the PA?
options: On 1 June itself
At least 30 days before 1 June
Within 30 days after 1 June
Within 12 months after 1 June
quiz.explanation: For a first-time appointment, the BA 020 must be submitted at least 30 days before the appointment becomes effective. Filing on or after the start date breaches the rule.

quiz.question: A proposed director is a South African national. His criminal background check report is dated 45 days before the BA 020 is submitted. What is the problem?
options: Reports must be no older than 7 days for anyone
Reports for South Africans are not required at all
Reports may be up to 12 months old for South Africans, so the issue is the missing CV
A South African's report may be at most 30 calendar days old
quiz.explanation: Directive 7 of 2022 sets 30 calendar days for South African nationals and 60 for foreign nationals, measured from the date the BA 020 is submitted. A 45-day-old report is too old for a South African.

quiz.question: A nominee refuses to undergo a criminal background check, saying his reputation speaks for itself. What does Directive 7 of 2022 say?
options: He is disqualified for appointment to the position
The bank may appoint him if two directors vouch for him
He may serve for six months while the PA decides
The check can be replaced by a sworn affidavit
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 2.1.4 says a person unable or unwilling to undergo a check is disqualified. No vouching or affidavit alternative is offered.

quiz.question: Sable Crest completes a periodic re-screening of its serving executive officers on 3 March. When must the reports reach the PA?
options: Only at the next annual BA 020 cycle
Within 7 days, by registered post
Only if a report shows a conviction
Within 30 calendar days of completing the screening
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 2.1.13 requires periodic re-screening and submission of the reports within 30 calendar days of completing it. All results go, not only adverse ones.

quiz.question: A director's background check shows an old minor conviction he did not disclose on his BA 020. What is the best governance response?
options: Remove the report from the file because the conviction is old and minor in nature
Appoint him and update the form at the next annual review
Correct the form, assess both issues and give the PA the full picture
Ask the PA informally whether to mention it at all
quiz.explanation: The bank is responsible for an honest fit and proper assessment and the PA considers probity. Non-disclosure is itself relevant. Hiding or delaying it would undermine the chair's submission.

quiz.question: Which finding did the VBS investigator report to the PA in October 2018?
options: The board had met all fit and proper requirements but was misled by outside auditors
Three non-executive directors admitted they had been improperly rewarded
The bank's losses were caused by a cyber attack
The audit committee had stopped the fraud in 2016
quiz.explanation: The Great Bank Heist report records that three non-executive directors confessed to improper rewards and that no honest person occupied the audit committee chair. It shows why probity must be re-tested over time.

quiz.question: Which body helps the board keep a continuity programme and regularly review the skills mix the board needs?
options: The audit committee under section 64
The PA's licensing department
The directors' affairs committee under section 64B
The remuneration committee under section 64C
quiz.explanation: Section 64B gives this role to the directors' affairs committee, whose skills reviews should feed both nominations and the directors' training plans.

quiz.question: The board's assessment finds that most directors struggle to question the bank's cyber and IT risk reports. What should follow under the governance policy?
options: Targeted training on that topic, recorded and rechecked at the next assessment
Replacing all directors who lack IT degrees
Leaving cyber matters to the chief information officer and the IT committee alone
Waiting for the PA to point it out in its review
quiz.explanation: Directive 1 of 2026 requires ongoing training and ongoing assessment; linking the two is how a bank shows its policy works. Replacing the board or delegating oversight away does not meet the duty of care and skill.

sessions.title: Health and safety at work: the OHS Act duties
sessions.summary: Apply the Occupational Health and Safety Act to a bank: the employer's general duty and its training duty in section 8(2)(e), the duty to inform, employees' duties, the CEO's responsibility, health and safety representatives and committees, and how inspectors enforce the Act.
objectives: Explain the employer's general duty in section 8 and the training duty in section 8(2)(e)
Apply the duty to inform in section 13 and employees' duties in section 14
Explain the CEO's responsibility under section 16 and the limits of delegation
Apply the rules on health and safety representatives and committees in sections 17 to 19

cards.title: Stage four: the fire door
cards.setting: Sable Crest regional office, Foreshore, Cape Town. 10:05.

lines.text: Look at this. A fire door wedged open with a box of archive files, and the evacuation map still shows last year's floor plan.
Is that really the bank's problem? It's a branch, not a factory.
The Occupational Health and Safety Act covers every employer, banks included. An office worker can still die in a fire.
And the duty isn't only about equipment. Section 8 says information, instructions, training and supervision.
Which makes it a governance issue too. Stage four: what the Act asks of the bank, its CEO, its managers and every employee.

cards.title: The OHS Act in five scenes

scenes.heading: One general duty
scenes.narration: Section 8 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act, 85 of 1993, says every employer must provide and maintain, as far as reasonably practicable, a working environment that is safe and without risk to employees' health.

scenes.heading: What that includes
scenes.narration: It includes safe systems of work and equipment, finding out what the hazards are and what precautions are needed, and eliminating or reducing hazards before falling back on protective equipment.

scenes.heading: Information and training
scenes.narration: Section 8(2)(e) is the training duty: the employer must give the information, instructions, training and supervision needed, as far as reasonably practicable, for employees' health and safety at work.

scenes.heading: The chief executive
scenes.narration: Section 16 makes the chief executive officer responsible for ensuring, as far as reasonably practicable, that the employer's duties are properly carried out. The CEO may assign duties but stays responsible.

scenes.heading: Everyone's part
scenes.narration: Section 14 asks every employee to take reasonable care, cooperate, follow safety rules and report unsafe situations and incidents quickly.

cards.title: Who does what under the OHS Act

items.label: Safe environment
items.right: Employee takes reasonable care for self and others (s 14(a))

items.label: Information and training
items.left: Employer gives what is necessary (s 8(2)(e), s 13)
items.right: Employee follows the rules and lawful instructions (s 14(c))

items.label: Unsafe conditions
items.right: Employee reports them as soon as practicable (s 14(d))

items.label: Incidents
items.left: Employer reports certain incidents to an inspector (s 24)
items.right: Employee reports by the end of the shift where possible (s 14(e))

cards.caption: Summarised from the Act as published in Government Gazette 14918 (2 July 1993).

cards.question: Which provision of the OHS Act expressly requires the employer to provide information, instructions, training and supervision?
options: Section 8(2)(e)
Section 17(5)
Section 24(1)
Section 7(1)
cards.explanation: Section 8(2)(e) lists these four as part of the employer's general duty, as far as reasonably practicable. Section 17 deals with safety representatives, section 24 with incident reports and section 7 with a written policy when the chief inspector directs it.

cards.title: 'As far as reasonably practicable' and section 13
cards.body:
Most duties in sections 8 and 13 are qualified by **"as far as is reasonably practicable"**. That is not a loophole. It means weighing how serious and likely the harm is against what is known about the hazard and the cost and availability of ways to reduce it. For ordinary office risks the precautions are usually cheap and well known, so excuses are weak.

**Section 13, the duty to inform**, adds that the employer must, as far as reasonably practicable:

- make every employee **conversant with the hazards** of their work and the precautions to take;
- tell the **health and safety representatives** in advance about inspections or inquiries an inspector has notified, and about exemption applications; and
- inform the relevant representative **as soon as reasonably practicable** after an incident in their area.

In a bank, typical hazards include fire and evacuation, electrical equipment, workstation strain, slips and trips, cash-handling and robbery risk, and travel between sites. The Act does not set a training frequency: the bank decides, based on risk.

cards.title: Whose duty is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each action under the OHS Act.

items.text: Give staff the information and training needed to work safely
Report a frayed cable under a desk as soon as practicable
Inspect the workplace at intervals agreed with the employer
Make sure work is supervised by someone trained to understand its hazards
Follow the branch's evacuation procedure during a drill
Investigate an employee's complaint about safety at work
Report an injury to the employer by the end of the shift where possible
Identify hazards and decide what precautions are needed

lines.text: My East London branch has 26 staff. Do I need a health and safety representative?
Section 17: more than 20 employees at a workplace means the employer designates representatives in writing. For shops and offices, at least one for every 100 employees or part of 100.
And the designation, functions and training of representatives happen during ordinary working hours, counted as work time.
We've never had one. Since we went over 20 staff two years ago.
Then we fix that now, and we tell Busi. It goes in the governance file.

cards.title: The missing representative
cards.situation: Thabo's East London branch has 26 employees and no designated health and safety representative. The annual internal audit starts next month. Thabo suggests appointing his deputy informally and backdating a letter.

choices.text: Consult staff in good faith on nominating or electing a representative, designate them in writing for a set period, arrange training in working hours and report the gap honestly.
choices.outcome: Best. Section 17 requires written designation after good-faith consultation, and section 18 entitles representatives to the training they reasonably need. Owning the gap is better governance than hiding it.

choices.text: Backdate a designation letter for the deputy so the audit finds no gap.
choices.outcome: Poor. A false record turns a compliance gap into dishonesty and still leaves the branch without a properly chosen, trained representative.

choices.text: Appoint the deputy in writing today without consulting staff.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Written designation is needed, but section 17 expects good-faith consultation with employees on how representatives are chosen. Skipping it invites a dispute and weak buy-in.

cards.title: OHS Act numbers to know

items.label: Representatives needed
items.detail: More than this many employees at a workplace triggers designation.

items.label: Shops and offices
items.detail: At least one representative for every 100 employees or part of 100.

items.label: Committee meetings
items.detail: A health and safety committee meets as often as needed, and at least this often.

items.label: Incident reports by staff
items.detail: An employee reports an injury incident by the end of the shift, where possible.

cards.caption: From sections 14, 17 and 19 of the Act as published in 1993. Check the current consolidated Act and regulations for later amendments.

cards.title: Match the section to its rule
cards.prompt: Link each OHS Act section to what it requires.

pairs.right: Employer's general duty: safe environment, hazards, information, training and supervision
Make employees conversant with hazards; keep representatives informed
The CEO must ensure the employer's duties are properly discharged
Committee where two or more representatives exist, meeting at least every three months
Report serious incidents to an inspector in the prescribed way

cards.question: The CEO of Sable Crest delegates all health and safety duties to the head of facilities in writing. What is the legal effect under section 16?
options: The CEO is no longer responsible for safety
The CEO may assign duties but keeps responsibility, and the bank keeps its liability
The head of facilities becomes the legal employer
The delegation is invalid unless an inspector approves it
cards.explanation: Section 16(2) lets the CEO assign duties to people under their control, but without derogating from the CEO's own responsibility, and section 16(3) keeps the employer's liability in place.

cards.title: Real case: inspectors and their notices
cards.body:
The Department of Employment and Labour enforces the OHS Act through inspectors. In a joint blitz inspection in Rustenburg, North West, in March 2024, the department reported issuing about **28 more notices** (contravention, prohibition and improvement) and **31 compliance orders** on a single day, and said it would keep bringing non-complying employers to book. The blitz tested compliance with the OHS Act alongside other labour laws.

That blitz was in wholesale and retail, not banking. But the tools are the same for any employer, including a bank branch:

- an **improvement** or **contravention** notice requires the employer to fix a problem;
- a **prohibition** notice can stop the use of a workplace or activity where conditions are hazardous.

**For Sable Crest:** an inspector visiting a branch with blocked fire exits, no representative and no training records would find the gaps in minutes.

cards.title: Training records that count
cards.body: For each employee keep: **induction safety briefing** (evacuation routes, assembly point, reporting), **role-specific training** (first aiders, fire marshals, cash-in-transit or robbery procedures), **refresher dates** you set from your risk assessment, and **drill records**. The Act sets no fixed frequency, so write your own and follow it.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: Section 8 makes every employer, including a bank, keep the workplace safe as far as reasonably practicable.
Section 8(2)(e) requires the information, instructions, training and supervision employees need; no frequency is set.
Section 13 requires employees to be made conversant with hazards and precautions.
The CEO must ensure the duties are discharged and stays responsible even after delegating (s 16).
Workplaces with more than 20 employees need written designation of representatives; offices need at least one per 100.

cards.prompt: Walk through your own workplace in your mind. Which hazard would a new colleague not know about on their first day, and who would tell them?

quiz.question: Does the Occupational Health and Safety Act, 85 of 1993, apply to a bank's offices and branches?
options: No, it applies only to factories and mines
Yes, its duties apply to every employer, offices included
Only if the bank uses heavy machinery
Only to branches that handle cash
quiz.explanation: Section 8 places its general duty on every employer, and section 17 even sets a specific ratio of representatives for shops and offices. Banks are covered.

quiz.question: Which phrase qualifies most employer duties in sections 8 and 13 of the OHS Act?
options: Subject to the employer's budget
Only where an inspector has issued a notice
As far as is reasonably practicable
Within the limits of the employer's insurance
quiz.explanation: The Act repeatedly uses 'as far as is reasonably practicable', which weighs risk against the means available to reduce it. It is not tied to budget, notices or insurance.

quiz.question: How often does the OHS Act say employees must receive safety training?
options: Once a year, by statute
Every three months, at the meeting of the health and safety committee
Only once, at induction
It sets no fixed interval; the employer gives what safety requires
quiz.explanation: Section 8(2)(e) requires necessary information, instructions, training and supervision but sets no interval. The bank should set refresher periods from its own risk assessment.

quiz.question: A new teller starts at Sable Crest's Durban branch. Under section 13, what must the employer do as far as reasonably practicable?
options: Make her conversant with the hazards of her work and the precautions to take
Give her a copy of the Act and ask her to sign it
Wait until the next annual drill to brief her
Register her with the Department of Employment and Labour
quiz.explanation: Section 13(a) is about making each employee conversant with the hazards and the precautions. Handing over the Act or waiting for a drill does not achieve that.

quiz.question: An employee trips over a loose carpet strip and sprains a wrist at 10:00. Under section 14, when should she report it?
options: Within 30 days, in writing
As soon as practicable, and by the end of that shift if she can
Only if she needs more than 14 days off work, through her line manager
Only if a colleague saw the fall
quiz.explanation: Section 14(e) requires an employee involved in an injury incident to report it as soon as practicable, no later than the end of the shift, unless circumstances made that impossible.

quiz.question: Sable Crest's Pretoria head office has 450 employees. What is the minimum number of health and safety representatives for that office under section 17(5)?
quiz.explanation: For shops and offices the minimum is one per 100 employees or part of 100. 450 employees means four full hundreds plus a part, so at least five representatives.

quiz.question: Sable Crest has three health and safety representatives at its Cape Town office. What follows under section 19?
options: It must set up a committee that meets at least every three months
Nothing, committees are optional for offices
It must replace the three representatives with one full-time safety officer
It must ask an inspector to chair monthly meetings
quiz.explanation: Where two or more representatives are designated at a workplace, section 19 requires one or more committees, meeting as often as needed and at least once every three months.

quiz.question: A branch manager wants safety representative training to happen on Saturdays, unpaid, to avoid disrupting the branch. Why is this a problem?
options: Training of representatives is the inspector's job under the Act, so the employer need not arrange it
Representatives may not receive any training under the Act
Saturday training is banned by the Banks Act
Section 17(7) puts representatives' training in ordinary working hours, as work time
quiz.explanation: Section 17(7) treats time reasonably spent on these activities as working time and places them in ordinary working hours; section 18(3) also requires the employer to provide the training reasonably required.

quiz.question: The CEO says: 'I delegated safety to the facilities manager, so the Act no longer applies to me.' What is correct?
options: The CEO is right once the delegation is in writing
Only the board chair is responsible under the Act
The facilities manager becomes the employer for the purposes of the Act once appointed in writing
The CEO may assign duties but stays responsible, and the bank stays liable
quiz.explanation: Section 16 makes the CEO responsible for ensuring the employer's duties are discharged; subsection (2) allows assignment without removing that responsibility, and subsection (3) keeps the employer's liability.

quiz.question: Which approach best reflects section 8(2)(b) when a branch finds that staff hurt their backs lifting coin boxes?
options: Remove or reduce the hazard, such as with trolleys, before relying on protective gear
Issue back-support belts and continue as before
Ask staff to sign a statement that they lift coin boxes at their own risk from now on
Record it and wait for an inspector's advice
quiz.explanation: Section 8(2)(b) requires taking reasonably practicable steps to eliminate or mitigate a hazard before resorting to personal protective equipment. Waivers do not remove the employer's duty.

sessions.title: Harassment prevention and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: Apply the Employment Equity Act and the 2022 Harassment Code: what harassment and sexual harassment are, where protection applies, policies, procedures, confidentiality and employer liability. Then pull the whole quest together into a readiness review for the PA and labour inspectors.
objectives: Explain harassment as unfair discrimination and the Code's test for sexual harassment
Identify the forms and settings of harassment the Code covers
Apply the Code's expectations on policy, procedures, confidentiality and training
Prepare evidence that the bank's governance, safety and harassment programmes work in practice

lines.text: A teller from the East London branch emailed me last night. A regional manager keeps sending her late-night messages about her looks, and hinted her promotion depends on 'being friendly'.
That's my branch. She never said anything to me.
She may not have felt she could. He's senior to you both.
This is where the board's governance meets one person's dignity. And it's our last stage before the PA's review.
Then let's get it right: what harassment is, what the Code expects of us, and how we prove our whole programme works.

cards.title: Harassment law in South Africa in five scenes

scenes.heading: Unfair discrimination
scenes.narration: Section 6(3) of the Employment Equity Act says harassment of an employee is a form of unfair discrimination, prohibited on any of the grounds listed in section 6(1), such as race, gender, sex, sexual orientation or disability.

scenes.heading: The 2022 Code
scenes.narration: The Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Harassment in the Workplace was published on 18 March 2022 under the Employment Equity Act. It guides employers and employees on all forms of harassment.

scenes.heading: What harassment is
scenes.narration: The Code describes harassment as unwanted conduct that impairs dignity, creates a hostile or intimidating environment or is meant to induce submission, and is linked to a prohibited or arbitrary ground.

scenes.heading: Where it applies
scenes.narration: Protection covers the workplace and work-related settings: trips, training and social events, work messages and online platforms, and transport the employer provides. Clients, suppliers and contractors can be harassers or victims too.

scenes.heading: Employer liability
scenes.narration: The Code explains that employers must take proactive and remedial steps under section 60 of the Act. An employer that fails to act adequately on a complaint can be held liable for the harasser's conduct.

cards.title: The test for sexual harassment in the Code

items.label: Prohibited ground
items.detail: Is it on the grounds of sex, gender or sexual orientation?

items.label: Unwanted
items.detail: Was the conduct unwanted or unacceptable? Silence does not mean consent.

items.label: Nature and extent
items.detail: Physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature; one incident can be enough.

items.label: Impact
items.detail: Did it impair dignity, considering the employee's circumstances and the parties' positions?

cards.caption: Item 5.3 of the 2022 Code lists these four factors.

cards.question: The regional manager says he never heard the teller object, so his messages cannot be harassment. What does the Code say?
options: He is right: harassment requires a clear objection
Conduct can still be harassment if he knew or ought to have known it was unwanted
Only physical contact can be sexual harassment
Only repeated conduct over six months counts
cards.explanation: The Code says a complainant not indicating the conduct is unwanted does not mean there was no harassment where the perpetrator ought to have known it could be regarded as unwanted. Verbal and electronic conduct count, and a single incident can be enough.

cards.title: Forms of harassment in the Code

cards.back: Using power over hiring, promotion, training, pay or discipline to coerce someone into sexual advances.
A person in authority rewarding those who respond to their sexual advances.
Punishing or intimidating someone for refusing advances or for complaining.
Abuse of coercive power by a person or group, often through repeated aggressive behaviour.
Harassment by a group of people aimed at one or more individuals.
Harassment through phones, email, social media or other technology; online bullying is cyber-bullying.
Unwanted conduct linked to race, ethnic or social origin, persistent or a single incident.

cards.title: What the Code expects of employers
Does the Code cover it?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each situation falls within the Code's scope.

items.text: Crude comments in the team's work WhatsApp group on a Sunday
A customer repeatedly propositions a teller at the counter
Unwanted touching at the bank's year-end function
A supplier's driver making racial remarks to branch cleaners
A manager's remarks during a work trip to Bloemfontein
A dispute between two neighbours who happen to work at different banks
An argument at a private family wedding unrelated to work

cards.title: Turning point: what the teller wants
cards.setting: Small meeting room, East London branch. 14:00.

lines.text: Thank you for trusting us. You can choose an informal route, where he is told clearly the conduct must stop, or a formal grievance and disciplinary process.
She's scared she'll lose the promotion either way.
Our policy and the Code are clear: she won't face adverse consequences for choosing either route, and victimising her would itself be a disciplinary offence.
One more thing. HR tells me two other staff raised similar concerns about him last year. That changes our duty.

cards.title: The second and third complaint
cards.situation: The teller asks for the informal route only: she wants the messages to stop and no hearing. HR has records of two earlier, similar concerns about the same regional manager. He manages 60 staff across four branches.

choices.text: Respect her choice for her own matter, but assess the risk to others; given the pattern, follow a formal procedure, explain why to her and protect her identity as far as possible.
choices.outcome: Best. The Code lets complainants choose, but where an investigation shows a significant risk of harm to others, considering severity and history, the employer must follow a formal procedure regardless, and tell the complainant.

choices.text: Follow the informal route only, as she asked, and close the file.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Her wishes matter, but closing the file ignores the earlier complaints. The Code expects the employer to assess the risk to others and act on it.

choices.text: Move the teller to another branch so she no longer reports to him.
choices.outcome: Poor. Moving the complainant punishes her, may count as victimisation and does nothing about the conduct or the risk to others.

cards.title: Real case: the Constitutional Court in McGregor (2021)
cards.body:
The 2022 Code itself relies on case law. It cites the Constitutional Court's judgment in **McGregor v Public Health and Social Development Sectoral Bargaining Council and Others [2021] ZACC 14**, a sexual harassment dismissal case involving a senior hospital doctor.

As the Code summarises it, the Court:

- **reiterated that the seniority of a perpetrator and a large age gap** between the perpetrator and the complainant are **aggravating factors** in sexual harassment; and
- recognised that people who experience harassment may describe themselves as a **complainant, survivor or victim**, or none of these, and that their choice deserves respect.

**For Sable Crest:** a regional manager's seniority over a junior teller does not soften the case. It makes it more serious, and the bank's response, including any sanction, should reflect that.

cards.title: Match the Code item to the duty
cards.prompt: Link each part of the 2022 Code to what it asks.

pairs.right: Guiding principles: zero tolerance, risk assessment, awareness training
Adopt and communicate a harassment policy with minimum statements
Clear informal and formal procedures, advice, sanctions and referral
Confidentiality of grievances, with safety steps still allowed
Include harassment in orientation, education and training

cards.title: Assessment readiness: where Sable Crest stands

items.label: Board training and BA 020 files
items.detail: Strong: training log per director, BA 020s with background checks.

items.label: Safety drills and committee minutes
items.detail: Strong: quarterly committee minutes and drill records at head office.

items.label: Tenure tracking
items.detail: Gap: nine-year dates not yet tracked for every independent director.

items.label: Branch representatives and harassment training
items.detail: Gap: one branch without a representative; orientation coverage untracked.

cards.caption: A self-assessment the company secretariat brings to the board before the PA's governance review.

cards.question: Which statement about training under the 2022 Harassment Code is most accurate?
options: It sets a binding annual training hour target for every bank
It expects employers to include harassment in orientation, education and training, as good practice
It applies only to employers with a trade union
It requires the PA to approve harassment training content
cards.explanation: Item 13 says employers should include sexual and other harassment in orientation, education and training in an accessible format. It is a code of good practice, so treat it as an expected competence rather than a fixed statutory course; it sets no hours.

cards.title: Before the review: the company secretary's checklist
steps: Map each obligation: Banks Act, Directive 1 of 2026, Directive 7 of 2022, OHS Act, Harassment Code
Collect evidence: policies, minutes, training logs, BA 020s, designations, drill and grievance records
Test the evidence against each requirement and list the gaps honestly
Agree remediation owners and dates, and report them to the board
Track closure and update the training plan for directors and staff

cards.title: Recap: what supervisors will ask
cards.body:
**PA:** Is your governance policy board-approved and implemented? Show director training and assessment records, independence declarations, tenure tracking and BA 020 files with background checks.

**Labour inspectors:** Show risk assessments, training and supervision records, designated representatives, committee minutes and incident reports.

**CCMA or courts, in a harassment dispute:** Show the policy, how you communicated it, the training given and how you handled the complaint.

cards.title: Stage five take-aways
items: Harassment is unfair discrimination under section 6(3) of the Employment Equity Act.
The 2022 Code covers all forms of harassment, in work-related settings, by and against staff, clients and suppliers.
Employers should adopt and communicate a policy, offer confidential informal and formal procedures and protect complainants from victimisation.
An employer that fails to act adequately on a harassment complaint can be held liable for the harasser's conduct.
Readiness means mapping each duty, holding evidence, admitting gaps and fixing them with owners and dates.

cards.prompt: If a colleague told you tomorrow that a senior person was harassing them, what would you say in the first two minutes, and where would you take it next?

quiz.question: Under the Employment Equity Act, how is harassment of an employee classified?
options: As a form of unfair discrimination prohibited on the listed grounds
As a criminal offence only, outside labour law
As a matter for the Banks Act and the PA
As a breach of contract with no statutory basis
quiz.explanation: Section 6(3) of the EEA, quoted in the 2022 Code, makes harassment a form of unfair discrimination on any of the section 6(1) grounds. Some harassment may also be criminal, but that is not its EEA classification.
